slides: Let's continue with team questions, and learn the V method.

slides.say: Now a method that does all this thinking for us. It's called the V method.
We use the same table. The question mark is in row two, in the time column.
Now we draw a V. It starts at the team in row one, goes down to the work in row two, and up to the time in row one.

slides: So the V joins six, forty and two.

slides.say: The rule is, multiply the three numbers on the V, and divide by the other two.
On top, six times forty times two. At the bottom, thirty times four.
at: On top, six times forty times two

slides.say: Let's cancel first. Forty divided by four is ten.
at: Forty divided by four is ten

slides.say: So on top, six times ten times two. At the bottom, thirty. Six times ten times two is a hundred twenty.
at: So on top, six times ten
Six times ten times two is

slides.say: And a hundred twenty divided by thirty is four. So four hours, the same as with ratios.
at: And a hundred twenty divided by thirty

slides: And we didn't have to think about the directions at all. The V does the same flipping for us. We don't need to prove it.

slides.say: The V must join three numbers. So it depends on where the question mark is.

slides: When the question mark is in the team or the time, we use the V like before.

slides.say: But when the question mark is in the work, the V turns upside down. Let's see an example.
The same six cooks make thirty pies in two hours. How many pies do four cooks make in six hours?
Now the V starts at the team in row two, goes up to the work in row one, and down to the time in row two. So it joins four, thirty and six.
at: Now the V starts at the team in row two

slides.say: On top, four times thirty times six. At the bottom, the other two, six times two.
at: At the bottom, the other two

slides.say: The sixes cancel. Four times thirty is a hundred twenty. And a hundred twenty divided by two is sixty pies.
Does it make sense? There are fewer cooks, but they work three times as many hours. So more than thirty pies makes sense.
So when do we use which? When only one thing changes, ratios are quick.
For example, the same job with twice the time needs only half the workers.
When two things change, the V does the thinking for us.

slides: Either way, the table always comes first. Team, work, time.

slides.say: So let's sum it up. Identical workers with a constant rate, in a group, means a team question.
at: Identical workers with a constant rate

slides.say: We put it in a table. Team, work, time, with the work in the middle.
at: We put it in a table

slides.say: With ratios, a change that goes the same way stays as it is. A change that goes the opposite way gets flipped.
With the V, we multiply the three numbers on the V, and divide by the other two.
And when the work is asked, the V is upside down.

slides: Take a moment to memorize this, and I'll see you in the next video.
